name: Prize crossword No 23,047
preamble: Next Monday (January 26) is Australia Day. So all but three of the Down solutions should be entered in the diagram as from down under.

clue.text: Sad Aussie detailed to bury digger's tool inside mountain

indicators.note: something in a sad state is in poor shape, so these letters are knocked out of their order
read as de-tailed, it means the tail is cut off, so the last letter goes
to bury something is to put it inside, so one piece goes into the other

blocks.note: Aussie with its final letter removed
a loy is a narrow Irish spade

explanation.surface: A miserable Australian is set to bury a digger's spade inside a mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is ALOYSIUS: Mount Aloysius is in Western Australia. A loy is an old Irish spade. As the preamble asks, this Down answer is entered bottom-up, reading SUISYOLA.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Aloysius is a peak in remote Western Australia, so the name alone stands for that particular summit.

clue.text: Mislaid keys of the cooler

indicators.note: things mislaid end up out of place, so these letters are put back in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone has lost the keys to the cool box.
explanation.walkthrough: An Esky is the Australian brand name for a portable picnic cool box. As the preamble says, this Down answer goes into the grid from the bottom up, so the grid reads YKSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Esky is the everyday Australian word for an insulated portable box that keeps drinks and food chilled.

clue.text: Dr Seuss heartless to, that is, a whiner

indicators.note: with the heart gone only the two ends of the word remain

blocks.note: a doctor is an MO, medical officer
only the first and last letters of the name

explanation.surface: Dr Seuss is dismissed as heartless by a complainer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dr Seuss' reads as one name, but Dr and Seuss are worked separately. The answer MOSSIE is entered bottom-up as the preamble asks.
explanation.definitionFit: Mossie is Australian and British slang for a mosquito, an insect famous for its high-pitched whine at night.

clue.text: Broken Hill team misses opening: what a record!

definitions.note: describes the answer through the phrase it usually forms, an all-time record

indicators.note: missing the opening means losing the first letter
something broken is in pieces, so the letters are put together again differently

explanation.surface: A sports side from the mining town of Broken Hill fails to get started, setting quite a record.
explanation.walkthrough: Broken Hill is a mining town in New South Wales, but here 'Broken' is the anagram signal. This is one of the three Down answers entered normally.
explanation.definitionFit: An all-time record is the best ever achieved, so the exclamation 'what a record!' points to that unbeaten superlative.

clue.text: Man at bay

blocks.note: first meaning: old British slang for a chap or fellow
second meaning: a small sheltered inlet of the coast

explanation.surface: A man is cornered, held at bay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At bay' looks like an idiom for being cornered; the two words are separate meanings. This is one of the three Down answers written normally.
explanation.definitionFit: Cove is dated British slang for a fellow, and also a small curved inlet of coastline.

clue.text: Film star Harris takes out Wilde's topless Mrs

indicators.note: to take someone out is to escort them, so one piece goes along wrapped by the other
with the top gone, one end letter is dropped; in a Down entry written upwards the top is the word's end

blocks.note: Mrs Erlynne in Lady Windermere's Fan, without her final E

explanation.surface: An actor named Harris dates Oscar Wilde's wife, who is undressed.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is ERROL FLYNN, the Tasmanian-born swashbuckler. Mrs Erlynne is the woman with a past in Wilde's Lady Windermere's Fan. Because Downs go in bottom-up, the E at the end of her name sits at the top.
explanation.definitionFit: Errol Flynn was a Hollywood leading man of the 1930s and 1940s, famed for swashbuckling roles like Robin Hood.

clue.text: Odds of a French team being seen in Northern Territory's land

definitions.note: the answer plus 'land' names the region

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters, first, third, fifth and so on, are kept

blocks.note: letters 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 of the run of words

explanation.surface: A French side is quoted betting odds while playing up in the Northern Territory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odds' looks like betting, but it means odd letters. The answer ARNHEM goes in bottom-up per the preamble.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnhem Land is the large Aboriginal-owned region in the north-east of the Northern Territory, named after a Dutch ship.

clue.text: How to avoid paying for a platypus?

blocks.note: second meaning: another name for the platypus

explanation.surface: Someone wonders how to get a platypus without paying for it.
explanation.walkthrough: To duck something is to dodge it, so ducking a bill avoids payment; split differently, the same letters name the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The platypus has a broad flat snout like a duck's beak, hence its common name, duck-billed platypus.

clue.text: The full measure of Australia

blocks.note: surface reading: the true size or extent of a country
setter's reading: Australia is nicknamed Oz, and Oz is also the abbreviation of a unit of weight; the full measure is that unit spelled out

explanation.walkthrough: Australians call their country Oz, which is also the written abbreviation of a small imperial weight; the clue asks for that abbreviation in full.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation oz stands for a unit of weight equal to one sixteenth of a pound, roughly 28 grams.

clue.text: Kangaroo, say, poetically heard in passage

indicators.note: what is heard is what the ear takes in, not the spelling

blocks.note: a passage between seats in a church or theatre

explanation.surface: A kangaroo is heard poetically in a narrow way through.
explanation.walkthrough: Kangaroo Island lies off South Australia; 'say' marks it as an example, and 'poetically' because isle is the literary word for island.
explanation.definitionFit: Isle is a poetic or literary form of island, and Kangaroo Island is one example of such a place.

clue.text: The Voice of the Highlanders?

definitions.note: names a regiment, the Sutherland Highlanders

blocks.note: first meaning: Dame Joan, the great Australian soprano
second meaning: the 93rd Regiment, raised in a Scottish Highland county of that name

explanation.surface: Someone asks who speaks for the Scottish Highlanders.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a spokesperson for Scots, but it is two separate things sharing one name: a singer and a Highland regiment.
explanation.definitionFit: Joan Sutherland was celebrated as La Stupenda for her soprano, and the Sutherland Highlanders were a Scottish army regiment.

clue.text: Brit takes headless cat back in to tree-dweller

indicators.note: without its head, a word loses its first letter
going back means running the letters the other way
to take something in is to hold it, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: Australian slang for a British person

explanation.surface: A Briton brings a decapitated cat back indoors to a tree-dwelling creature.
explanation.walkthrough: Pom, or Pommy, is the Australian nickname for a Briton.
explanation.definitionFit: Possums are Australian marsupials that live largely in trees, nesting in hollows and coming out at night.

clue.text: Soap he rubs on, GI-style

indicators.note: doing something in a new style means rearranging it, so the letters take another form

explanation.surface: An American soldier lathers himself with soap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soap' looks like what he rubs on, but it is the definition: the long-running Australian TV soap opera NEIGHBOURS, entered bottom-up.
explanation.definitionFit: Neighbours is a long-running Australian television soap opera set on Ramsay Street, hugely popular in Britain too.

clue.text: Mats laid out in bundles for dancing?

indicators.note: spread out means scattered around, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Mats are spread out in bundles, ready for a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: A matilda is a swagman's bundle of belongings; 'dancing' alludes to the song Waltzing Matilda, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian slang a matilda is a swag, the rolled bundle a tramp carries, famously sent waltzing in the song.

clue.text: Cry heard by 28 when not in court?

blocks.note: first meaning: a line judge's call heard by a tennis player such as Ken Rosewall
second meaning: a ball landing beyond the lines

explanation.surface: A tennis player hears a call when the ball misses the court.
explanation.walkthrough: 28 refers to 28 Across, ROSEWALL, the Australian tennis player. The answer OUT is entered bottom-up per the preamble.
explanation.definitionFit: Umpires shout 'Out!' when a ball lands outside the lines, so it is both the call and the state of the ball.

clue.text: Snap up a mixture of northerly 13

indicators.note: a mixture blends ingredients together, so the letters come out in a new order

explanation.surface: Grab a blend of something from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snap up' looks like the definition, meaning grab, but it is fodder. 13 points to 13 Down, NEIGHBOURS: Papua New Guinea lies just north of Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Papuans live in Papua New Guinea, the country directly north of Australia across the Torres Strait, so they are its neighbours.

clue.text: One that 20 made scores of

blocks.note: surface reading: something a person produced by the dozen
setter's reading: 20 is Don Bradman, and what a batsman scores is counted one at a time

explanation.surface: Something a famous figure turned out by the dozen.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 Down is BRADMAN, the great Australian cricketer; scores here are both twenties and cricket totals. The answer goes in bottom-up.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a batsman's tally is counted in single units gained by running between the wickets, and Bradman amassed thousands.

clue.text: Making fast, low sound

blocks.note: to low is what cattle do

explanation.surface: Something makes a quick, deep noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like speed and 'low' like pitch; here fast means secure and low means the cow's call.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a boat fast is to tie it securely, which is exactly what tying up at a quay or buoy involves.

clue.text: Nationality of a citizen from Western Australia

blocks.note: first meaning: belonging to the Balkan country
second meaning: someone from Albany, a port town in Western Australia

explanation.surface: A form asks the nationality of a Western Australian resident.
explanation.walkthrough: Albany is a town on the south coast of Western Australia, so a resident could be called by the same word as a Balkan national. Entered bottom-up.
explanation.definitionFit: The demonym serves both the European country of Albania and, playfully, the Western Australian town of Albany.

clue.text: Don underwear? Damn ridiculous!

indicators.note: something ridiculous is absurd and disordered, so the letters lose their sensible order

explanation.surface: Someone is told to put on underwear and protests that it is absurd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like the verb for putting clothes on, but it is a first name: Sir Don Bradman, Australia's greatest batsman. Entered bottom-up.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Donald Bradman, universally called the Don, was the Australian cricketer with a Test batting average of 99.94.

clue.text: Can an airline go wrong internally and make capital?

indicators.note: something happening internally takes place inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: to err is to make a mistake

explanation.surface: Could an airline's internal mishap end up turning a profit?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make capital' looks like making money, but 'capital' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Canberra is the purpose-built seat of the Australian federal government and the nation's capital city.

clue.text: Be quiet and lie back with a bird!

indicators.note: going back means reading in the opposite direction

explanation.surface: Someone is told to hush and lie down with a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' looks like a feathered creature, but it is British slang for a young woman. The answer SHEILA goes in bottom-up.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheila is Australian slang for a woman, matching the British slang use of bird for a girl or girlfriend.

clue.text: Chunder-making! Quote me! Send it back!

indicators.note: returning something sends it the way it came, so the letters run the other way

explanation.surface: Something sick-making, with demands to be quoted and to return it.
explanation.walkthrough: Chunder is Australian slang for vomit.
explanation.definitionFit: An emetic is a substance that induces vomiting, so it is literally something that makes a person throw up.

clue.text: Where Cook put a horse to work

indicators.note: putting something to work reshapes it, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cook sets a horse to work somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Cook is Captain James Cook, who landed at Botany Bay in 1770; to put ashore is to land from a ship. The answer goes in bottom-up.
explanation.definitionFit: Ships' crews put ashore when they land, which is what Cook's party did on reaching Australia's east coast.

clue.text: Did you redecorate (as some say) the Tube?

indicators.note: the way some people say it means pronunciation counts, not spelling

blocks.note: a broad pronunciation of the question

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether you have redone the London Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Tube' looks like London's Underground railway, but it is the long wooden pipe played by Aboriginal Australians.
explanation.definitionFit: The didgeridoo is a long hollowed wooden pipe blown to make a droning sound, essentially a musical tube.

clue.text: Australian sailors and I find a princess

explanation.surface: Some Aussie sailors and the speaker discover a royal lady.
explanation.walkthrough: This is one of the three Down answers entered normally, top to bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: A rani is a Hindu queen or princess, the wife of a raja or a female ruler in her own right.

clue.text: Magda you'll find inside, morning and afternoon, I'd say

indicators.note: what you find inside is already there within the words, waiting to be read

explanation.surface: Magda can be found indoors in the morning and afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: G'day is the classic Australian greeting, used at any time of day, which is why one word covers both morning and afternoon.
explanation.definitionFit: The Australian greeting is short for good day, said where others would say good morning or good afternoon.

clue.text: Has Wagga the heart for such a man?

definitions.note: the answer plus man gives the swagman who carries it

indicators.note: the heart is the core, so the letters sit in the middle of the words

blocks.note: runs across the end of one word and start of the next

explanation.surface: Does Wagga have the courage for such a fellow?
explanation.walkthrough: Wagga Wagga is a town in New South Wales. A swag is the rolled bedding of an itinerant, and the one who carries it is a swagman. Entered bottom-up.
explanation.definitionFit: A swag is the bundle of belongings an Australian tramp carries, the very thing that makes him a swagman.

clue.text: Wolf down chow mein with no starter; William drops out

indicators.note: with no starter there is no opening letter
whatever drops out is removed from inside the remaining letters

blocks.note: the dish without its first letter
Wm is the standard abbreviation of the name, and these letters are removed

explanation.surface: Someone bolts a Chinese meal without the first course, and William quits.
explanation.walkthrough: Hoe in is Australian slang for tucking in to food eagerly.
explanation.definitionFit: To hoe in is to eat heartily and greedily, much like gobbling or devouring a meal.

clue.text: Ken who served well, or as badly

indicators.note: something done badly comes out wrong, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A man named Ken served either well or badly.
explanation.walkthrough: Ken Rosewall was an Australian tennis champion of the 1950s to 1970s; 'served' points to tennis, not military service.
explanation.definitionFit: Ken Rosewall won eight Grand Slam singles titles, serving in tennis matches across three decades.
